Look at your wristwatch.
Is a second really
the same everywhere in
the universe?
Physics says no.
For two hundred years,
almost everyone believed
in the universe of
Isaac Newton.
In 1687, Newton wrote
that time flows steadily
and equally for everything,
independent of anything else.
In his picture,
one second in London
was the same as
one second on Mars.
Time was a silent
backdrop for the drama
of matter and motion.
If you dropped an
apple from an English
tree, it fell under
gravity, but the ticking
of the universe stayed
pure and untouched.
That tidy universe came
crashing down in the
early twentieth century,
when a young Swiss
patent clerk named Albert
Einstein looked deeper
into the nature of light.
The speed of light
in a vacuum is
an unbreakable cosmic speed
limit, about 299,792
kilometers per second.
And it never changes,
no matter how fast
you move toward or
away from the beam.
In 1905, Einstein took
that fact seriously,
and it led to
a shocking consequence.
If the speed of
light must be identical
for everyone, then distance
and time themselves must
bend to make it so.
Ten years later,
in 1915, Einstein went
further with his theory
of general relativity.
Space and time are
not separate.
They are woven into
one four-dimensional fabric
called spacetime.
Gravity is not an
invisible force reaching
across empty space.
Gravity is the warping
of spacetime by mass
and energy.
The heavier an object
is, the deeper it
dents the fabric of
reality around it.
That warping leads to
one of the strangest
effects in physics:
gravitational time dilation.
When a massive object
curves spacetime, it changes
not only the shape
of space but the
rate at which time passes.
Clocks deeper in a
gravitational well run
measurably slower than
clocks farther away.
In 2010, physicists at
the United States National
Institute of Standards
and Technology measured
this on Earth,
using clocks lifted just
thirty-three centimeters
apart.
Stand at the bottom
of a steep spacetime
valley, and you travel
into the future more
slowly than someone standing
on the plateau above.
Time is not a river.
It bends.
And the most extreme
bend of all is
waiting near a black hole.
